blocks.text:
Design a Movie Ticket Booking System where users can book seats for a specific show. The system must guarantee that a seat is never sold to two different bookings, and must correctly calculate the total price across every seat type in a booking.

  • Actors: users booking one or more seats for a single show.
  • Scope: one show with a fixed seating layout, seat-type-based pricing, and booking confirmation.
  • Goal: guarantee no seat is ever double-booked, and every booking’s price exactly matches the seats actually reserved.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: a seat can be part of at most one confirmed booking, ever. Every other requirement builds on top of that guarantee.

items: The system shall let a user request a booking for one or more specific seats on a show.
The system shall reject a booking if any requested seat is not currently available.
The system shall calculate the total price based on each seat’s type.
The system shall mark every seat in a successful booking as permanently booked.
The system shall notify listeners of both successful and failed booking attempts.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: no double booking, pricing consistency, extensibility and observability

items: No double booking: a seat must never end up part of two different confirmed bookings, this is the single most important guarantee in the whole system.
Consistency: the price charged must always exactly match the type of every seat actually booked.
Extensibility: new seat types and new pricing rules (like weekday vs weekend pricing) must be addable without rewriting the booking flow.
Observability: every booking outcome, success or failure, must be visible to anything watching the system.
Thread Safety: two users requesting the same seat at nearly the same moment must never both succeed.
Should a partial booking be allowed if only some of the requested seats are available, or must the whole request succeed or fail together?
How long should a "locked" (mid-checkout) seat remain reserved before automatically releasing if payment is never completed?
Should pricing support more than a fixed per-seat-type rate, like demand-based or time-based pricing?
Do we need to support cancelling a confirmed booking, releasing its seats back to available?
Is a single show enough, or do we need to support many shows and theaters simultaneously?
A booking request for multiple seats is all-or-nothing, if even one requested seat is unavailable, the entire request fails and nothing is locked or charged.
This design implements a fixed StandardPricingStrategy, the pricing mechanism itself is pluggable for future strategies.
Seat locking here represents the checkout window, in this simplified design a lock immediately proceeds to booking, a production system would add a timeout and release logic.
Booking cancellation is discussed as follow-up work, not implemented in the core flow.
This design covers a single show, a real system would layer Theater and Movie entities above it, discussed in Improvements.

metadata.alt: BookingService composing a Show (which aggregates Seats), a PricingStrategy, and notifying BookingObservers

items: Seat: one physical seat, its type, and its current status.
Show: one screening, holding every seat that belongs to it.
PricingStrategy: however a seat’s price gets decided.
BookingObserver: anything that wants to react to a booking succeeding or failing.
BookingService: the orchestrator running the whole check-lock-price-confirm flow.

metadata.alt: BookingService composing a Show, which aggregates every Seat that belongs to it

items: Composition: BookingService composes its Show, the show has no purpose outside the specific booking session using it.
Aggregation: Show aggregates its Seat objects, a seat conceptually exists as part of the show’s layout.
Association: BookingService is associated with a PricingStrategy and zero or more BookingObservers, both swappable independently.
Realization: StandardPricingStrategy realizes PricingStrategy; ConsoleBookingObserver realizes BookingObserver.

metadata.alt: BookingService tying together Show, Seat, PricingStrategy and BookingObserver

blocks.text: Notice that Seat itself has no booking logic at all, all of the check-lock-confirm sequencing lives entirely in BookingService. This keeps Seat a simple, predictable data holder.
Three patterns keep this design correct and genuinely extensible.

metadata.alt: PricingStrategy as the shared contract behind a fixed-rate strategy and a future demand-based strategy

blocks.text: Why needed: pricing rules vary widely between systems, fixed per seat type today, demand-based or time-of-day-based tomorrow. Why best: BookingService only ever calls pricingStrategy.getPrice(seat), it never needs to know how that number was decided. What it solves: lets pricing evolve independently of the booking flow itself.

metadata.alt: BookingService notifying every registered BookingObserver of both successful and failed bookings

blocks.text: Why needed: a real system needs to send confirmation emails, update analytics, and refresh a UI, all in reaction to the same booking outcome, without BookingService needing to know any of them exist. Why best: new observer types can be added freely with zero changes to the booking flow itself. What it solves: keeps notification concerns fully decoupled from booking logic.

metadata.alt: ScreenLayoutFactory generating a full seating layout from just two counts

blocks.text: Why needed: manually constructing dozens or hundreds of Seat objects by hand for every show would be repetitive and error-prone. Why best: ScreenLayoutFactory centralizes exactly how a layout’s seat ids and types are generated, in one tested place. What it solves: makes creating a new show’s seating layout a single, reliable method call.

items: Seat: responsibility is holding an id, type, and current status. Attributes: id, type, status. Methods: getId(), getType(), getStatus(), setStatus().
Show: responsibility is owning every seat for one screening and providing lookup by id. Attributes: id, seats (map). Methods: getSeat().
BookingService: responsibility is running the entire booking workflow correctly. Attributes: show, pricingStrategy, observers, bookingCounter. Methods: bookSeats(), addObserver().

metadata.alt: PricingStrategy and BookingObserver as the two extension points, each with one concrete implementation shown

blocks.text: PricingStrategy isolates how a price is calculated, letting pricing rules evolve independently. BookingObserver isolates reactions to booking outcomes, letting any number of independent systems watch the same booking service.
Three workflows matter most: a successful booking, a failed booking, and the safety guard preventing a race condition.

metadata.alt: Two available seats being checked, locked, priced, and confirmed as one atomic booking

blocks.text: Every step happens in strict order, availability is fully verified before anything is locked, and nothing is locked before pricing is calculated.

metadata.alt: A booking request rejected immediately because one of its seats is no longer available

blocks.text: The failure happens at the very first check, before any seat is touched, this is exactly why a failed booking never partially locks or charges anything.

metadata.alt: Two users requesting the same seat, with the second request correctly rejected once the first completes

blocks.text: This is the concurrency guarantee made concrete: whichever request actually acquires the lock first proceeds all the way through, and the second sees the seat as already booked, never as still available.

metadata.alt: The full booking sequence: check availability, lock, price, then confirm or fail

items: Happy path: every requested seat is available, all are locked, priced, and confirmed as one successful booking.
Failure, seat unavailable: at least one requested seat is not AVAILABLE, the entire request is rejected before anything is locked.
Failure, unknown seat id: a requested seat id does not exist on this show at all, treated identically to an unavailable seat.
BookingService.bookSeats(List seatIds): the single entry point for attempting a booking, returns the new booking id or null/None on failure.
BookingService.addObserver(BookingObserver): registers a new observer for booking outcomes.
Show.getSeat(String seatId): the core lookup every booking check is built on.
ScreenLayoutFactory.createLayout(regularCount, premiumCount): the only way seat layouts are built in this design.

metadata.alt: A booking request containing an unknown seat id being rejected before any seat state changes

items: Invalid input: a seat id that does not exist on the show is treated the same as an unavailable seat, the booking is rejected before anything changes.
Resource unavailable: a seat already LOCKED or BOOKED by another request causes an immediate, safe rejection.
Business-rule violation: a partial booking (some seats available, some not) is never allowed to partially succeed, the all-or-nothing check happens before any locking begins.
System failure: a broken booking observer throwing an exception should be caught per-listener, never allowed to prevent a valid booking from actually confirming.

metadata.alt: Two users requesting the same seat, guarded by a lock around the entire availability-check-and-reserve sequence

blocks.text: bookSeats() reads and writes seat status across multiple steps (check, then lock, then confirm), if two requests for the same seat run concurrently, both could pass the availability check before either locks anything. The entire check-and-lock sequence must be synchronized (ideally per-seat locking for better throughput, or a single lock around bookSeats() for simplicity) so only one request can ever transition a given seat out of AVAILABLE.

items: Adding demand-based pricing (prices rising as a show fills up) requires only a new PricingStrategy implementation, zero changes to BookingService.
Adding an EmailConfirmationObserver that sends a real confirmation email is a pure BookingObserver implementation.
Supporting seat lock expiry (auto-releasing a LOCKED seat if checkout is abandoned) would add a timestamp to Seat and a background sweep, without changing the core bookSeats() flow.
Future work: layering Theater and Movie entities on top of Show would let one system manage many screenings across many theaters, reusing this exact booking flow unchanged per show.
Single Responsibility: Seat only tracks its own state, Show only owns its seat collection, BookingService only orchestrates the booking workflow.
Open/Closed: new pricing strategies and observer types can be added without modifying BookingService’s existing, already-correct logic.
Liskov Substitution: any PricingStrategy or BookingObserver implementation can be substituted freely without BookingService needing to know which one it has.
Interface Segregation: PricingStrategy exposes exactly one method, BookingObserver exposes exactly the two events it genuinely needs.
Dependency Inversion: BookingService depends on the PricingStrategy and BookingObserver abstractions, never on a specific concrete implementation.
A booking request with an empty seat list: should be rejected or treated as a no-op, never silently "succeed" with a zero-price booking.
The exact same seat id appearing twice in one booking request: must not be double-counted in pricing or double-locked.
A show with zero seats: still a technically valid Show, every booking attempt against it simply fails immediately.
A booking request submitted the instant after a show has already ended: out of scope for this core design, discussed as follow-up work around show lifecycle.
Show.getSeat(): O(1), a direct hash map lookup by seat id.
BookingService.bookSeats(): O(k) where k is the number of seats in the request, every step (check, lock, price, confirm) is a single pass over the requested seats.
ScreenLayoutFactory.createLayout(): O(regularCount plus premiumCount), directly proportional to the layout size.
Space: O(total seats) for the show’s seat map, O(k) additional space per booking request.

metadata.alt: SHOW containing SEAT rows, with BOOKING and BOOKING_SEAT capturing which seats belong to which booking

blocks.text: SHOW stores the screening itself, SEAT tracks every seat’s type and current status for that show, BOOKING records a confirmed transaction with its total price, and BOOKING_SEAT is the join table linking a booking to every seat it actually includes, since one booking can cover multiple seats.

items: How would you implement automatic seat lock expiry so an abandoned checkout releases its seats back to available?
How would you extend this design to support Theater and Movie entities managing many shows across many screens?
How would you support booking cancellation and refunds, releasing previously booked seats?
How would you scale seat locking across multiple servers without a single in-memory lock becoming a bottleneck?

items: Why check availability for ALL requested seats before locking ANY of them? Because locking one seat and then discovering a second is unavailable would leave the first seat pointlessly locked, checking everything upfront keeps the operation cleanly all-or-nothing.

Why is a LOCKED status needed at all, why not go straight from AVAILABLE to BOOKED? Because a real system needs a window for payment processing, LOCKED represents "reserved but not yet paid," a genuinely necessary intermediate state.

Why does BookingService hold seat lookups through Show rather than directly holding a list of Seat objects itself? Because Show is the natural owner of "which seats exist for this screening," BookingService should only know how to run the booking workflow, not manage seat inventory itself.

An alternative could use optimistic locking (a version number per seat, checked and incremented atomically) instead of an explicit LOCKED status, better for high-throughput distributed systems, more complex to reason about for a teaching-oriented design.
A simpler design could skip the LOCKED intermediate state entirely and go straight to BOOKED, simpler code, but leaves no window to actually process payment before committing the seat.

Using a message queue to serialize all booking requests for a given show would avoid explicit locking altogether, a legitimate production pattern, but adds infrastructure complexity not needed at this design’s scope.
Add a background job that releases LOCKED seats back to AVAILABLE if checkout is not completed within a reasonable timeout.
Persist every booking and seat status change (already modeled in the ER diagram) so bookings survive a server restart.
Rate-limit booking attempts per user to prevent a single client from repeatedly locking and abandoning seats.
Expose a read-only seat map API separately from bookSeats(), so a UI can show live availability without risking accidental mutation.
